When an RL researcher and an LLM-agent builder say *agent*, they name different objects, and claims that cross between them arrive with the words but not the objects: a deployed LLM agent is said to hack a reward it does not have. This paper lays the two meanings side by side, one primitive at a time, in training and in deployment, and says where each word keeps its meaning and where it loses it. It describes the gap and proposes no bridge.

In deployment, the RL agent's task still has a reward function, written by its designer, whether or not the frozen policy uses it; the deployed LLM's task has none, and its objective is the instruction in the context.
Neither a deployed RL policy nor a deployed LLM uses reward to change its parameters; that difference is between training and deployment, not between the cultures.
In training and in deployment alike, an LLM agent's observations can carry instructions it may follow; an RL agent's cannot.

In training and in deployment alike, an LLM agent's behaviour can be changed by natural-language instructions in its input without changing parameters; the RL settings here assume no such instruction channel, excluding RL policies conditioned on natural-language goals.
A deployed RL environment may be designed to reset; no LLM deployment setting is.
